extracted.intended_audience: novelists and fiction writers (also critics and students of narrative technique)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling narrative method (first person, third person, epistolary, dramatization of consciousness) in novels so that character, action, and inner life are most effectively rendered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of first-person narrator when hero is central
rubrics_metrics.description: The young man Harry ... is only a recorder, a picture-maker, so long as he speaks for himself. He is expected to lend us his eyes (which he does), and yet at the same time to present himself for us to behold with our own; the subject of his story requires no less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person narration is useful for describing the world through a particular eye, but it cannot both 'lend us his eyes' and simultaneously present a searching, elaborate portrait of the narrator himself. If the main weight of the story falls in the narrator's own life or inner history, first person will touch and pass its limit; dramatization or another method should be used so the reader can 'get behind his description and judge for ourselves.' Examples: Meredith's Harry (limited), Copperfield and Esmond (less burdened), where first person suffices for pictorial description but not for fully dramatized inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize a character's consciousness when it is the story's center
rubrics_metrics.description: What it was like to be Harry ... with all that action and reaction of character and fortune proceeding within him — that is the question, the chief question; ... Drama we want, always drama, for the central, essential, paramount affair, whatever it is; Harry’s consciousness ought to be dramatized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the chief subject of the novel is the inner life of a character, represent that inner history as drama (action) rather than relying on retrospective report. The reader should experience the mind 'in the act of judging and reflecting' rather than only being told about it. Examples of successful dramatization: Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov, Henry James's Strether.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use third-person dramatization that makes the hero's mind visible
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist returns to the third person again, but he returns with a marked difference. ... instead of receiving his report we now see him in the act of judging and reflecting; his consciousness ... is now before us in its original agitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a third-person stance that still renders the world 'in the hero’s terms' but shows the hero's interior life 'in the act' so that the mind becomes a dramatic phenomenon. This allows the mind to 'appear' and 'act' on the page while preserving the novelist's power to picture widely and take a broad view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: avoid personal narrator when living drama is possible
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal narrator will do very well and may be extremely helpful, so long as the story is only the reflection of life beyond and outside him; but as soon as the story begins to find its centre of gravity in his own life ... his report of himself becomes a matter which might be strengthened, and which should accordingly give way to the stronger method. No reflection, no picture, where living drama is possible — it is a good rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rule, do not let the hero narrate his own central emotional/dramatic material if that narration blocks immediate dramatic presentation of events or inner action—unless there is a specific artistic reason (e.g., ironic self-revelation in Barry Lyndon). When violated, critics look for particular causes that make it appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: push dramatization only as far as the subject allows
rubrics_metrics.description: The method is to be pushed as far as the subject can profit by it, but no further. It may happen (for instance in David Copperfield) that the story needs no high dramatic value, and that it would get no advantage from a more dramatic method. If it would gain nothing, it would undoubtedly lose; the subject would be over-treated and would suffer accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the degree of dramatization economically. Over-treating a subject by forcing heightened dramatic method can displace the subject and harm the book; under-treating can leave it unsubstantial. Let the subject indicate the ideal point on the line toward drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer an indirect/circuitous method to produce a straighter effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The prudent novelist tends to prefer an indirect to a direct method. The simple story-teller begins by addressing himself openly to the reader, and then exchanges this method for another and another, and with each modification he reaches the reader from a further remove. The more circuitous procedure on the part of the author produces a straighter effect for the reader; that is why, other things being equal, the more dramatic way is better than the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use layers of narrative distance (e.g., narrator-character-authorial removal) to let the thing itself appear more directly to the reader. Let method be guided by the subject to achieve the most immediate impression possible without explicit authorial telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the story speak for itself (show, don't explain)
rubrics_metrics.description: He wishes the story so far as possible to speak for itself, the people and the action to appear independently rather than to be described and explained. To this end the method is raised to the highest dramatic power that the subject allows, until last ... there need be no revelation of anybody's thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for scenes and behavior that allow readers to infer motives and emotions rather than supplying explanation. Even necessary description should be treated so it gains the value of drama. Sometimes no interior revelation is needed if the scene can do the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary/diary method to capture contemporaneous emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of making a story out of a series of letters, or a running diary written from day to day — is engaged in the attempt to show a mind in action, to give a dramatic display of the commotion within a breast. He wishes to avoid throwing Clarissa’s agitations into the past and treating them as a historical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use letters or diaries when the subject is the contemporaneous unfolding of feeling and conduct (Clarissa) — this keeps suspense and makes emotion immediate. But beware: the method strains verisimilitude, can force contrived plot maneuvers to keep characters apart, and may become impracticable for large-scale narratives (Grandison example). Consult exemplars (Clarissa, Grandison) for detail and pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize thought by representing its surface movement
rubrics_metrics.description: The world of silent thought is thrown open, and instead of telling the reader what happened there, the novelist uses the look and behaviour of thought as the vehicle by which the story is rendered. The impulses and reactions of his mood are the players upon the new scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat impulses, reactions, 'the movement that flickers over the surface of his mind' as dramatic elements — use them to render inner processes without authorial exposition. This is akin to theatrical technique where hidden motives must be shown through looks, tones, and deeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the subject is wholly pictorial (one man's vision), tell from that point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a purely pictorial subject, covering Strether’s field of vision and bounded by its limits; it consists entirely of an impression received by a certain man. There can accordingly be no thought of rendering him as a figure seen from without; nothing that anyone else could discern ... would give the full sense of the eventful life he is leading within.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a novel's essential subject is the particular impression or vision of a single consciousness, structure the narrative to deliver that vision (share Strether’s vision). External action and other characters are meaningful only insofar as they are seen by that mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pass responsibility from author to in-book agents (narrators/characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus it becomes clear why the prudent novelist tends to prefer an indirect to a direct method ... The fiction that he devises is ultimately his; but it looks poor and thin if he openly claims it as his, or at any rate it becomes much more substantial as soon as he fathers it upon another. 'This is not my story,' says the author; 'you know nothing of me; it is the story of this man or woman ...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overt authorial intrusion; present the tale as arising from another person in the book so the material appears more substantial and self-contained. Be mindful that the narrator's authority remains a question; readers may still require evidence (dramatization) to accept the narrator's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of autobiography: a man cannot fully objectify himself
rubrics_metrics.description: No man can completely objectify himself, and a credible account of anything must appear to detach it, to set it altogether free for inspection. The novelist passes on towards drama, gets behind the narrator, and represents the mind of the narrator as in itself a kind of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on autobiographical narration to give a 'thoroughly valid' account of complex mental processes; supplement or replace with dramatized scenes that detach and make inner life inspectable.
